 IBM's latest batch of 'Night Hawk'
 to be installed on Yonsei-generation quantum computers
For the first time, it is important for Korea to secure its own original technology
" to be wary of competition for introduction in a hurry." 사진 확대 IBM Quantum System One, a quantum computer installed at Yonsei University International Campus in Songdo, Incheon. [Picture = Yonsei University] IBM's "Night Hawk," the world's best quantum computer processor, has entered Korea. It is the first time in the world that it will be introduced to a facility outside the United States.
 Analysts say that South Korea is taking off as a global quantum base by actively introducing overseas quantum computers. However, balancing the introduction of overseas products and development of its own technology remains a task for the future.
 Yonsei University announced on the 4th that it has introduced the latest IBM quantum processor, "Night Hawk," at the Songdo International Campus Quantum Computing Center. It will be installed on IBM's quantum computer 'Quantum System One' introduced by Yonsei University in 2024.
 Originally, it was equipped with 'Eagle', a state-of-the-art processor at the time, but it is being upgraded again in two years. There was no additional cost as an extension of the contract two years ago.
 Currently the world's best quantum processor, the Nighthawk can handle 25 times more data than Eagle. Yonsei University aims to solve social problems by using quantum computers for ongoing research.
 Jeong Jae-ho, head of Yonsei University's quantum business, said, "It will be used for various purposes to solve many problems in the era of bio-new drugs, space, climate change, energy crisis, and artificial intelligence."
 Currently, only four universities in the world have introduced IBM quantum computers: Yonsei University, Tokyo University, and the Federal University of Technology in Zurich. Among them, IBM comprehensively evaluated the research results and the use of quantum computers, and Night Hawk was introduced to Yonsei University for the first time. An official from Yonsei University said, "As IBM researchers also use quantum computers installed at Yonsei University, Yonsei University's research and utilization capabilities have been well evaluated."
 With this introduction, Korea has established itself as a key hub for global quantum research. However, in order for Korea to leap forward as a true quantum power, there are voices that the introduction of foreign products and self-development must be well balanced. This is because if limited resources are used only to introduce foreign products, securing its own original technology will inevitably be delayed.
 Yonsei University spent 80 billion won on purchases two years ago, and its annual maintenance cost is about 100 million won. Some within Yonsei University criticized, "We have spent too much money even though the demand is not yet clear." Last year, Chungbuk National University also introduced Finnish IQM's quantum computer, and the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI) is currently building an IonQ quantum computer.
 There are also concerns about competitively introducing quantum computers in a situation where immediate performance is uncertain. "It is not desirable to introduce equipment competitively without sufficient plans considering the considerable cost," said Jeong Hyun-seok, a professor at Seoul National University. "It is time to put more weight on efforts to develop hardware in Korea rather than focusing on introducing finished products abroad."
 "The quantum computer strategy is similar to the strategy of introducing fighter jets," said Choi Jae-hyuk, head of the Quantum Technology Research Institute at the Korea Institute of Standards and Science. "We need to secure our own original technology while purchasing foreign products to be used immediately." Director Choi said, "We need to speed up securing the original technology because the timing of commercialization of quantum computers, which was expected to be around 2035, is moving forward by more than five years."
 The key is how to use the introduced quantum computer. This is because it can remain a latecomer or pioneer new markets depending on how it is used.
 Chung Hyeon-cheol, CEO of Norma, who combines self-development and overseas technical cooperation, said, "We should not remain at the level of making good use of purchased foreign equipment," adding, "The equipment introduced is also meaningful only when it is used as a springboard for accumulating domestic technology." "There are opportunities in the application market, such as combining quantum computers with AI," he said.
